In addition to submitting a proposed commission structure for in-app purchases (IAP) made through systems other than the App Store within the United States, Apple also filed a motion expressing its willingness to explore the possibility of a settlement with Epic Games. Details are as follows.

Apple may be ready to settle

Apple had previously submitted a proposal outlining the commission it hopes to be allowed to charge on transactions completed through payment systems outside the App Store.

The timing of Apple's filing came as the Supreme Court denied Apple's request to stay the lower court proceedings during its review of Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers' civil contempt ruling against Apple, which found Apple in contempt after it was ordered to allow developers to direct users to external payment methods yet continued to charge a 27% commission.

Under Apple's proposed framework, Apple could charge up to a 15% commission on transactions completed through alternative payment systems. Epic Games immediately objected, stating that it "believes these fees go far beyond the guidelines set by the Ninth Circuit for permissible fees."

Although that document attracted significant attention, Apple today also filed a separate motion asking Judge Gonzalez Rogers to order both parties to attend a settlement conference.

Excerpts from the document (edited for clarity):

That is to say, Apple's legal team had contacted Epic's lawyers before filing the motion to discuss applying for a settlement conference, but Epic did not agree to that request.

In the document, Apple pointed out that the court has the authority to order both parties to attend a settlement conference without Epic's consent, and added that the Ninth Circuit itself also encourages both parties to reach an agreement on appropriate external link commissions.

Apple also noted that "discussing potential settlement options in a confidential, non-adversarial environment will increase the likelihood of reaching a pragmatic solution, thereby avoiding a lengthy remand process."

It is worth noting that this document does not contain any settlement proposals or offers from Apple, nor does it constitute a genuine settlement proposal. Apple is actually asking the court to order both parties to conduct settlement negotiations under the supervision of Magistrate Judge Joseph C. Spero.
